attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post. He states it as fact.

semantics.note: Faithful paraphrase of a retrospective observation about Microsoft's stance toward OpenAI. The original has a typo ('have increasingly backing away'), but the meaning is clear.

contract.note: The plain reading (rival models, looser exclusivity, or pulled-back investment) is ordinary and fair. Whether 'backing' means money or product reliance decides the result, and the speaker did not say which.

evidence.note: Microsoft's own dated announcement that it added Anthropic models to M365 Copilot. It does say OpenAI models stay, but this is still real diversification.
June 16, 2026: Cowork is built on Anthropic technology, and a DeepSeek option is being weighed. This shows product sourcing moving away from OpenAI.
The license became non-exclusive in April 2026, but the context shows OpenAI pushed for the change. Under the contract, OpenAI-driven loosening does not cleanly show Microsoft backing away.
Microsoft kept a roughly 27% stake worth $135B and secured a $250B Azure commitment. No financial retreat is shown.
Strain ran both ways, and OpenAI's revenue chief complained about the partnership's limits. Some loosening was OpenAI's doing.

reviews.rationale: The product-reliance part holds: Microsoft added Anthropic models in 2025 and built Cowork on Claude technology by June 2026. The financial-backing part is not shown: Microsoft kept a roughly 27% stake and won a $250B Azure commitment, and no reduced investment is documented. The exclusivity loosening appears to have been driven largely by OpenAI.

attribution.note: Marcus relays Zitron's report but adopts it as fact, calling it 'the third bad thing'. The sentence is his own and he endorses it.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the qualifier that this is per Zitron's report. 'Bad news' reflects his framing. It is an observation about 2025 burn compared with what people expected.

contract.note: Reading 'burning money' as cash burn is its ordinary meaning, and the widely reported $8–8.5B target is a reasonable baseline for what people thought. The result turns on this choice of metric: read as operating loss or total spending, the claim might hold.

evidence.note: Reports 2025 out-of-pocket cash burn of about $8B, in line with expectations. It rests on unnamed sources, and other outlets label the figure differently.
Reuters, Sept 2025: the 2025 cash-burn target was $8.5B. This is the pre-leak baseline.
Reuters, Sept 2025: projected 2025 burn of over $8B. A second report of the baseline.
Operating loss was $20.9B. That is a different metric, including non-cash items, so it is context only.

reviews.rationale: On the contract's cash-burn reading, reported 2025 cash burn was about $8B, matching the earlier $8–8.5B expectation rather than exceeding it. The headline 8x loss and the $20.9B operating loss are different metrics, swollen by non-cash charges. One caveat: the $8B figure comes from unnamed sources and its definition is somewhat uncertain.

attribution.note: Marcus's own firm assertion in his post.

semantics.note: An unhedged claim that roughly 8x annual loss growth cannot continue for long. Read as a forecast with no stated horizon.

contract.note: It uses annual net losses, imposes no number of years and no tolerance, and requires completed annual accounts. That is fair and does not stretch the claim either way.

evidence.note: The March 2026 financing shows access to capital. It does not measure annual loss growth after 2025.
Q1–Q2 2026 quarterly operating losses. This is an interim, different metric and cannot settle annual net-loss growth.

reviews.rationale: No horizon was stated. No completed annual accounts for a year after 2025 exist by the evaluation date, and no event meets the early-resolution rule. Interim quarterly operating losses and financing news cannot settle the forecast.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words, building on a quoted tweet and his own earlier prediction. He endorses the claim.

semantics.note: The claim says no moat, with everyone building the same thing, has eroded OpenAI since January 2024, and that the share numbers show it. Causal kind is correct.

contract.note: Using market-share data with rival substitution as the test of the causal link is an ordinary reading. 'Ever since' January 2024 and the cause both depend on interpretation.

evidence.note: Similarweb: ChatGPT's share fell from 87.2% to 68% between Dec 2024 and Dec 2025 as Gemini rose.
Similarweb: about 64–65% in January 2026, down from about 86% a year earlier. It credits Gemini's gains partly to Google's ecosystem.
Similarweb: 52.7% in May 2026, down from 76.4%, with Gemini and Claude gaining.
Sensor Tower: 46.4% in May 2026, the source of the 'below 50%' figure. It also cites Department of War uninstalls and Google's ecosystem as factors.

reviews.rationale: Supported part: ChatGPT's share fell steeply from Dec 2024 to May 2026 as similar rivals gained, and the 'numbers' (below 50%) are real. Not supported: the packet has no data showing erosion during 2024, when share was still about 87% at year-end. The cause is also not isolated, since sources credit Google's distribution and the Department of War backlash too.
